title: How does Spark achieve fault tolerance through lineage (the DAG of transformations is recorded; if an executor loses a cached partition, Spark recomputes only that partition from its parent RDD, not the entire job)?

s1_definition.profdef: Spark achieves fault tolerance through lineage, which is the recorded directed acyclic graph of transformations that produced each RDD. Instead of replicating data for recovery, Spark remembers how every partition was derived from its parents. When an executor fails and a partition is lost, Spark does not restart the whole job; it looks up that partition's lineage and recomputes only the missing partition by re-applying its transformations to its parent partition, which is deterministic because RDDs are immutable and transformations are pure.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps, for every summary report, not a photocopy but the exact recipe: "take the raw transaction box, filter Rajesh's slips, total the amounts." If a clerk's desk catches fire and one summary page is destroyed, the manager does not redo the entire day's work and does not need a backup photocopy — he simply re-runs that one recipe on the original transaction box and reproduces exactly that one page. Because the recipe is written down and the raw box never changes, the rebuilt page is identical to the lost one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spark recovers from failures by replaying the recorded lineage recipe to recompute only the lost partitions, not by replicating data or rerunning the whole job.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark achieves fault tolerance through lineage, which is the recorded directed acyclic graph of transformations that produced each RDD. Instead of replicating data for recovery, Spark remembers how every partition was derived from its parents. When an executor fails and a partition is lost, Spark does not restart the whole job; it looks up that partition's lineage and recomputes only the missing partition by re-applying its transformations to its parent partition, which is deterministic because RDDs are immutable and transformations are pure.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps, for every summary report, not a photocopy but the exact recipe: "take the raw transaction box, filter Rajesh's slips, total the amounts." If a clerk's desk catches fire and one summary page is destroyed, the manager does not redo the entire day's work and does not need a backup photocopy — he simply re-runs that one recipe on the original transaction box and reproduces exactly that one page. Because the recipe is written down and the raw box never changes, the rebuilt page is identical to the lost one.

**One line to remember:** Spark recovers from failures by replaying the recorded lineage recipe to recompute only the lost partitions, not by replicating data or rerunning the whole job.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is that Spark records lineage for every RDD. Each RDD knows its parent RDDs and the transformation that derives it from them, so the full chain from the base data up to any RDD is captured as a directed acyclic graph. This graph is metadata held in the Driver; it is cheap to keep and does not store the data itself, only the recipe. That is the opposite of the classic Hadoop approach of replicating stored data for fault tolerance.

When an executor fails — because a machine crashes, a process is killed, or memory is exhausted — any RDD partitions that executor held, including cached ones, are lost. The Driver detects the failure through missing heartbeats and the failure of the tasks that were running there. Instead of failing the job, the DAGScheduler consults the lineage of the lost partitions. For each missing partition, it schedules a task that recomputes that partition by re-applying its transformation to the corresponding parent partition. Crucially, it recomputes only the lost partitions, not the entire RDD and not the whole job, because every other partition is still valid and present.

This recomputation is correct precisely because of immutability and purity. RDDs never change after creation, and transformations like map and filter are deterministic functions, so re-running the recipe on the same parent partition yields exactly the same result. If the parent partition itself was also lost, the scheduler recurses further up the lineage until it reaches partitions that still exist or the base data in reliable storage, then recomputes forward.

There are important nuances. First, narrow dependencies make recovery cheap because a lost child partition depends on just one parent partition, whereas wide dependencies are costlier because recovering a post-shuffle partition may require recomputing many parent partitions and re-running a shuffle. Second, very long lineage chains, as in iterative machine learning, make recomputation expensive because the recipe has hundreds of steps; this is exactly why checkpointing exists — it writes an RDD to reliable storage like HDFS and truncates the lineage so recovery starts from the checkpoint rather than the very beginning. Third, this is also why cache alone is not a durability guarantee: a cached partition is just a performance optimization, and if it is lost it is transparently recomputed from lineage. In my banking jobs, this meant a single node dying during a long aggregation caused a small, localized recompute rather than an expensive full restart.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — When a desk fails, redoing the entire day's processing is unacceptable. This is exactly why Spark recomputes only the lost partition from lineage.

Problem 2 — The rebuilt page must be identical to the original. This is exactly why immutability plus pure transformations make recomputation deterministic.

Problem 3 — A recipe with hundreds of steps is slow to replay after every failure. This is exactly why checkpointing truncates lineage.

The mini-project models lineage recovery in Java. `LineageRdd` stores a parent reference and the transformation, and can compute any partition by replaying its recipe. A `partition lost` event drops a cached partition; `recoverLostPartitions` recomputes only the missing ones. A `checkpoint` method materializes the current RDD and clears its parent to truncate lineage. The demo filters and maps Rajesh's transactions, simulates losing one partition, recovers it, then checkpoints and shows that recovery afterward is shallow.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions in two partitions — partition 0 has Rajesh Rs.1000 and Priya Rs.500, partition 1 has Rajesh Rs.3000.

Step 1: We build a lineage by filtering to Rajesh's transactions and mapping to amounts. Nothing has run; only the recipe is recorded with a parent chain base, filtered, mapped.

Step 2: We compute both partitions. Partition 0 replays the recipe on base partition 0 to yield Rs.1000, and partition 1 yields Rs.3000. Both results are cached in memory on their executors.

Step 3: An executor fails and partition 1 is lost. The cached Rs.3000 is gone, and the parent's cached copy on that executor is gone too. The log records a severe failure.

Step 4: Recovery runs for only partition 1. Spark replays the recorded recipe — read base partition 1, filter to Rajesh, map to amount — and deterministically reproduces Rs.3000. Partition 0 is untouched and the whole job is not restarted.

Step 5: We checkpoint the RDD, which materializes both partitions to reliable storage and clears the parent link, truncating the lineage. The RDD is now effectively a root.

Step 6: We lose partition 0 and recover it again, but this time recovery is shallow — it reads the checkpointed data directly rather than replaying the filter and map chain. The journey shows localized recovery from lineage and the role of checkpointing in keeping recovery cheap.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] p0=[1000], p1=[3000]
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [SEVERE] executor failure: cached partition 1 LOST
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] recomputing ONLY partition 1 from lineage (not whole job)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] after recovery p1=[3000]
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] checkpoint: materializing to reliable storage and truncating lineage
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [SEVERE] executor failure: cached partition 0 LOST
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] recomputing ONLY partition 0 from lineage (not whole job)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] after checkpointed recovery p0=[1000]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  base ──filter(SAV2001)──→ filtered ──map(amount)──→ mapped   (lineage recipe)
   P0                          P0                        P0=[1000] (cached)
   P1                          P1                        P1=[3000] (cached)

  ── Executor failure: P1 lost ──
  mapped.P1 = GONE
    │ consult lineage for P1 only
    ▼
  base.P1 → filter → map → [3000]   (recompute ONLY P1, job NOT restarted)

  ── After checkpoint (lineage truncated) ──
  mapped = root (materialized)      parent = null
  P0 lost → read checkpoint → [1000]  (shallow recovery, no filter/map replay)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Lineage-Based Fault Tolerance ═══

  ┌──────────┐  heartbeats  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │ Driver   │◀────────────│ Executors (hold cached parts) │
  │ holds    │  missed HB → │                               │
  │ lineage  │  failure     └─────────────┬─────────────────┘
  │ DAG      │                            │ executor dies → parts lost
  └────┬─────┘                            ▼
       │ DAGScheduler: for each lost partition, schedule recompute
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Recompute ONLY lost partitions by replaying lineage       │
  │   parent partition still present? → recompute forward     │
  │   parent also lost? → recurse up lineage                  │
  │   lineage truncated by checkpoint? → read reliable store  │
  └─────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
                ┌──────────────────────────┐
                │ HDFS/S3: base data +      │ ← checkpoint dir
                │ checkpoint snapshots      │
                └──────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Lineage + Recovery + Checkpoint ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Memento/Recipe: lineage stores how to rebuild, not the data │
  │     WHY: cheap fault tolerance without replication           │
  │  Recursive Composite: compute(p) recurses up the parent chain│
  │     WHY: rebuild from wherever valid data still exists        │
  │  Snapshot (checkpoint): materialize + truncate lineage        │
  │     WHY: bound recovery cost for long chains                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: LineageRdd models data + its recovery recipe             │
  │  O: new transformation = new recipe, recovery code unchanged │
  │  L: filtered/mapped RDDs recover identically to any RDD      │
  │  D: recipe is a Function abstraction, not hardcoded logic    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              LineageRdd<T>                 │
  │────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ - baseData: List<List<T>>  (root/checkpoint)│
  │ - parent: LineageRdd<Object>  ◆ lineage link │
  │ - recipe: Function<...>                     │
  │ - cache: Map<Integer,List<T>>  (losable)    │
  │────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ + map/filter : LineageRdd (lazy)            │
  │ + compute(p): List<T> (cache or replay)     │
  │ + losePartition(p): void                    │
  │ + recoverLostPartitions(Set<Integer>)       │
  │ + checkpoint(): void (truncate lineage)     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Partition ───────────────────────────────────

  [COMPUTED+CACHED] ──executor dies──→ [LOST]
        ▲                                 │
        │ recompute from lineage          │
        └─────────────────────────────────┘
  [CHECKPOINTED] ──lost──→ read reliable store ──→ [RESTORED] (shallow)

  ── Call Chain ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. LineageDemo.main()
  2.   → base.filter(...).map(...)   → lineage recorded
  3.   → compute(0), compute(1)      → cached [1000],[3000]
  4.   → losePartition(1)            → P1 LOST
  5.   → recoverLostPartitions({1})  → replay → [3000]
  6.   → checkpoint()                → truncate lineage
  7.   → losePartition(0) → recover  → shallow read → [1000]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark achieves fault tolerance through lineage, which is a fundamentally different approach from replicating data. For every RDD, Spark records the directed acyclic graph of transformations that produced it — the recipe for deriving each partition from its parents — and keeps this lineage as cheap metadata in the Driver. It does not store copies of the data for recovery; it stores how to rebuild it. When an executor fails and its partitions, including cached ones, are lost, the Driver detects it through missed heartbeats and failed tasks, and instead of restarting the whole job it consults the lineage of the lost partitions and recomputes only those, by re-applying their transformations to their parent partitions.

This works correctly because RDDs are immutable and transformations are pure, deterministic functions, so replaying the recipe on the same parent data produces exactly the same result. If a parent partition was also lost, the scheduler recurses further up the lineage until it reaches partitions that still exist or the base data in reliable storage. Narrow dependencies make this cheap because a lost child partition depends on just one parent partition, while wide dependencies are more costly because recovering a post-shuffle partition can require recomputing many parents and re-running a shuffle.

In my project at the National Bank of India this meant that a single node dying during a long aggregation caused only a small, localized recompute rather than an expensive full restart, which was essential for finishing nightly jobs on time. The one caution I always raise is that for deeply iterative work, like machine learning, lineage chains grow to hundreds of steps and replaying them after a failure becomes slow, so I used checkpointing to materialize an RDD to reliable storage like HDFS and truncate the lineage, which bounds recovery cost. It is also worth stressing that caching is only a performance optimization, not durability — a lost cached partition is simply recomputed from lineage transparently.
